sections.title: Referral + Alum
sections.timing: Within 2 to 3 days of being given the name.
format: Put the referrer’s name in the subject line and open the first sentence with it
Say how you know the referrer in the same sentence, in a clause rather than a paragraph
Fold the shared school into the introduction as a short phrase, not its own paragraph
Say why the referrer pointed you here specifically
One ask: a 10 to 15 minute call
Mention the resume once, thank them once, and sign off
notes: Never write “I found you in the alumni directory” when a referral is the actual reason you are writing
The school is a warm touch here, not the argument; the referral is the argument
Do not add “is there anyone else I should speak with” on top of the call ask

sections.title: Met in Person + Alum
sections.timing: Within 24 to 48 hours of the event.
format: Open on the specific moment: the event, the day, and what you talked about
Let the school arrive naturally, as something you learned afterward or noticed at the time
Say what stuck with you from the conversation
One ask: a 10 to 15 minute call
Mention the resume once, thank them once, and sign off
notes: The moment you met is the reason they will remember you, so it goes first and the school comes second
“I was glad to learn afterward that you are also a Larkfield alum” is one clause and does the whole job
Do not restate your entire background; you already met

sections.title: Campus Recruiter + Alum
sections.timing: Within 48 hours of the fair or event, or any time if you are writing cold.
format: Say where you met, if you did, in the opening line
Give your name, school, class year, and graduation date early
Mention the shared school once, as a warm touch rather than an argument
Ask two or three questions about programs, timeline, and how to prepare
One ask, the resume mentioned once, thank them, and sign off
notes: Never ask a recruiter about their own career path; they own the calendar and the process, and that is what only they can tell you
Two or three specific questions get answered, six do not
The shared school is worth exactly one clause here

sections.title: Coffee Chat Thank You + They Offered to Help
sections.timing: Within 2 to 3 hours of the conversation, while the offer is still live.
format: Thank them for the conversation and name one specific detail from it
Thank them for the exact offer they made, in their own terms
Make the offer easy to act on: attach the resume with the requisition number, or supply a three-sentence blurb
No second ask, and no “is there anyone else I should speak with”
Thank them once more and sign off
notes: They already gave you something, so adding a second ask converts a favor into a transaction
Attach the resume only if they asked for it or offered to pass it along
If they offered an introduction, write the blurb for them; three sentences they can paste is the whole gift

sections.title: Keep in Touch + Congratulations
sections.timing: Whenever you see their news, ideally 2 to 3 months after your last conversation.
format: Open by referencing your last conversation and roughly when it was
Give your update and tie it directly to advice they gave you
Congratulate them on their news, with a genuine reason it makes sense
No ask, or at most a light and pressure-free offer to catch up
Thank them and sign off
notes: The congratulations must be specific; “saw your news, congrats” reads as a pretext for the update
No referral ask, no resume, and nothing attached
Four short paragraphs at most

sections.title: Thanking the Person Who Introduced You + an Update
sections.timing: Within a day of the call happening.
format: Confirm that the call happened and when
Share one specific thing you learned from it
Fold in a short personal update since you last spoke
Say what is next for you
Thank them, and ask for nothing
notes: The purpose is to make the introduction feel worthwhile, so there is no room for a second request
One specific thing you learned proves the introduction was used well
Keep the update to a sentence or two; this email is about them, not you

sections.title: Referral + Met in Person
sections.timing: Within 24 to 48 hours of the meeting.
format: The referral opens the email, since it came first chronologically and carries more weight
The meeting follows in the same sentence or the next one, not in a separate paragraph
Say what stuck with you from the conversation you actually had
One ask: 10 to 15 minutes, the resume mentioned once
Thank them and sign off
notes: Two facts, one sentence: “Devin suggested I reach out, and I was glad to meet you at the panel before I got the chance”
Do not thank them twice for two different things; one thank you covers both
Since you have already met, cut your background to a single line

sections.title: Referral + Campus Recruiter
sections.timing: Within 2 to 3 days of getting the name.
format: Open with the referrer, exactly as in any referral email
Give your name, school, class year, and graduation date early
Move straight into two or three program questions about timeline, eligibility, or preparation
One ask, the resume mentioned once, thank them and sign off
notes: A referral to a recruiter is an invitation to ask process questions, not career questions
Never ask the recruiter about their own path, even with a referral in hand
Keep the referral to one sentence; the questions are what the email is for

sections.title: Met at a Conference + Campus Recruiter
sections.timing: Within 48 hours of the conference ending.
format: Name the conference and the city in the first line, since they attended it alongside hundreds of students
Give the placing detail: where you spoke and what about
State your school, class year, and graduation date
Ask two program questions, then one ask
Mention the resume once, thank them and sign off
notes: The placing detail matters more at a conference than anywhere else; they met a room, not a person
Recruiters at conferences take names, so the follow up is what converts a conversation into a record
Two questions, not five

sections.title: They Offered to Help + a Talk a Banker Gave
sections.timing: The same evening or the next morning.
format: Name the session, the date, and where it was held
Reference the point from their remarks that stuck with you, and the question you asked if you asked one
Thank them for the specific offer they made afterward
Make the offer easy to act on, and add no second ask
Thank them and sign off
notes: The offer usually comes in a hallway after the talk, so remind them of the moment as well as the session
No “anyone else I should speak with” on top of an offer they already made
Attach the resume only if the offer was to pass it along

sections.title: They Offered to Help + a Session a Recruiter Ran
sections.timing: The same evening or the next morning.
format: Thank them for running the session, not merely for attending it
Reference the specific thing they explained about the process
Thank them for the exact offer they made
Give them what they need to act: the requisition number, the resume, or the blurb
Thank them and sign off
notes: Recruiters organize these evenings and get thanked far less than the speakers do
Include the requisition number; it is the single most useful thing you can hand a recruiter
No process questions here, since this email is a thank you rather than an inquiry

sections.title: Thanking the Person Who Introduced You + Congratulations
sections.timing: Within a day of seeing their news, whenever the introduction has already happened.
format: Confirm the call happened and name one thing you learned
Congratulate them on their news with a genuine reason
Ask for nothing at all
Thank them and sign off
notes: This one must stay very short: roughly 110 words and four or five sentences
Two warm things in one email is the ceiling; a third makes it read as a setup for an ask
No resume, no attachment, no question

sections.title: Second Conversation + an Update
sections.timing: At least six weeks after the first call, or right before a deadline.
format: Reference the first conversation and when it was
Lead with what you did with their advice, since that is the argument for a second call
Let the update support that, rather than standing on its own
One ask: 15 minutes, with a reason for asking now
Thank them and sign off
notes: What you did with the advice is the core of the email; the update is evidence, not news
Give a reason for the timing, such as a deadline or the start of recruiting
Do not ask again if you did nothing with the first conversation

sections.title: Someone I Emailed Sent Me to Them + Alum
format: The first sentence names the person who redirected you and why they did
The shared school comes in briefly, in a clause
Say what you were originally asking about, so the redirect makes sense
One ask, the resume mentioned once
Thank them and sign off
notes: A redirect is a weaker signal than a referral, so be precise about who sent you and why
Do not overstate it: “Marcus suggested you would be better placed to answer this” is honest and enough
The school is the warm touch, not the reason

sections.title: Referral + Someone I Emailed Sent Me to Them
sections.timing: Within 2 days, once both names are in hand.
format: Name both people in one sentence, with the stronger connection first
Say in a clause what each of them was responding to
Give one line of background, then one ask
Mention the resume once, thank them and sign off
notes: Two names is the maximum before an email starts to read like a chain letter
Put them in one sentence: naming each in its own paragraph doubles the length and halves the effect
If both are lukewarm connections, lead with whichever one actually knows the recipient

sections.title: Three or More Boxes at Once
sections.timing: Whenever the situation genuinely stacks; the timing is set by the most recent event.
format: Pick the strongest single fact and give it the first sentence
Compress everything else into clauses attached to sentences that were already going to exist
Cut your background to one line, since the connections are doing that work
One ask, the resume mentioned once, one thank you
notes: What gets cut: your club list, your major’s explanation, the second thank you, and any “anyone else I should speak with”
What survives: the strongest connection, the moment you met, the reason you are writing, and the ask
If the email passes 200 words, cut a fact rather than trimming words evenly

sections.title: Thanking the Person Who Sent You Elsewhere + an Update or Congratulations
sections.timing: Within a day of the onward conversation happening.
format: Confirm that the onward call happened and thank them for the redirect specifically

Share one thing you learned, which shows the redirect was right - but only when THIS EMAIL says what came of the conversation. With nothing given, say the conversation was worth having and move on; never leave a bracketed marker in its place
Add either a short update or a congratulations, not both
Ask for nothing
Thank them and sign off
notes: People who redirect you rarely hear what happened, so this email is unusually memorable
Thank them for the judgment, not just for the name; sending you to the right person is the favor
Keep it under 150 words

sections.title: Second Conversation + Thanking the Person Who Introduced You
sections.timing: At least six weeks after the first call.
format: The ask for a second conversation leads the email
What you did with their advice is the argument for it
Fold the thanks for the introduction they made into a clause, not a second request
One ask: 15 minutes, with a reason for now
Thank them and sign off
notes: The thanks for the introduction must not turn into a request for another one
If you find yourself writing “and if you know anyone else”, delete the sentence
One ask, always

Hi Corinne,

Professor Linnet Ashgar, who advises my senior thesis at Larkfield, suggested I write to you. She mentioned that you took her seminar years ago and that you have built a career at the intersection of science and investing, which is the path I am trying to understand.

I am a junior at Larkfield studying molecular biology, so I come at this sideways. My thesis work on clinical trial design is what convinced me that the interesting decisions in healthcare are made by whoever is funding the trial, not running it. Professor Ashgar thought you would be the person to tell me whether that instinct is naive.

Would you have 15 minutes for a call in the coming weeks? I am glad to work entirely around your schedule, and my resume is attached for reference.

Thank you for your time!

Best,
